implementation_notes: java.base ships the pattern: AsynchronousSocketChannel and AsynchronousServerSocketChannel execute operations without blocking the caller and invoke a CompletionHandler when they complete, with the generic attachment carrying per-request state; an AsynchronousChannelGroup supplies the dispatcher threads and the concurrency strategy. Future-returning overloads and CompletableFuture composition cover the same model when callback style is awkward.
pitfalls: At most one read and one write may be outstanding per AsynchronousSocketChannel: a second read throws ReadPendingException, so a handler must wait for the completion before reissuing.
Completion handlers run on the channel group's threads: blocking inside one stalls that thread, and a short read reports only the bytes actually read, so the remainder must be requested again.
A timed-out read or write can leave the channel in an implementation-specific error state with undefined buffer contents (javadoc); the buffer must be discarded.

variants.name: Virtual threads over the blocking API
variants.implementation_notes: With virtual threads the completion dispatch disappears from the code: when code running in a virtual thread calls a blocking I/O operation in the java.* API, the runtime performs a non-blocking OS call and suspends the virtual thread until it can be resumed, as JEP 444 describes. The programmer writes thread-per-request code and the platform supplies the proactor, at the cost of having to avoid pinning and pooling.
pitfalls: Virtual threads that block inside synchronized blocks or native calls are pinned to their carrier, so long I/O there blocks the carrier; use ReentrantLock for hot paths.
Never pool virtual threads: create one per task and bound concurrency with semaphores instead.
Thread-per-request resource caching (thread-locals holding connections) stops amortising when every request gets a new thread.
